utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, before you could hear me, I wished good morning to everyone, so you've missed that. Good morning to you as well. Now, I see you can hear it. And Madam Registrar has called the case. Please be seated. May I have the appearances. The Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. For the Prosecution, Susan L. Somers, lead counsel; behind me, Ms. Gina Butler, Mr. Philip Weiner; to my right, Mr. Nicholas Kaufman and Miss Victoria McCreath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. And the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Ms. Somers. Eugene O'Sullivan, Jelena Nikolic, and Zarko Nikolic for Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. The order of this hearing today, which is a hearing in which we'll hear the submissions of the parties and evidence relevant for sentencing will be the following: First, the Prosecution will shortly introduce its position in regard of sentencing; then - and I understand that it takes less time for the Defence to do the same - this would take approximately 40 minutes altogether; we'll then hear the testimony of witnesses called by the Prosecution, as far as I understand, two witnesses to be examined in closed session. Ms. Somers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the parties agree on that, that it will be in closed session. Then we'll see a video to be presented by the Prosecution. And then there'll be a victim's address, as far as I understand, and that all before we hear the first Defence witness, then, and we'll hear another Defence witness. We'll then -- it's announced that Mr. Jokic will make an oral statement, and finally closing arguments will be presented by the parties, Prosecution first and then the Defence. I already announced at this moment that it may be that before we hear the first witness that we need a short break for reasons not related to this case, so that the parties are prepared that we might have a short additional break. I do understand that the parties also agreed on this order. So if there's nothing else to be -- to be submitted at this moment, I could give an opportunity to the Prosecution to present its position in regard of sentencing, but I'll not do that until I first have briefly set out what this case is about. This case is about the events that that happened the day after tomorrow 12 years ago, on the 6th of December, 1991, which was the shelling of the city of Dubrovnik, which caused the death of persons, which caused persons to be injured, and which caused serious damage to the old city of Dubrovnik. Now, Mr. Jokic, you have pleaded guilty in relation to these events on six counts, as they are in the indictment. That is the case on which we'll hear the submissions of the parties on sentencing and on which we'll hear evidence in relation to sentencing. MS. Somers, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Following up what Your Honour has presented as introductory comments, inasmuch as the Trial Chamber has not had the benefit of a tremendous amount of background evidence, the Prosecution will take a bit of time to put into context the events underlying the factual basis to which Admiral Jokic has entered his plea of guilty. The unlawful shelling attacks on the old town of Dubrovnik, this is focal point of this indictment, which occurred on the 6th of December, 1991, must be viewed as among the most shameful events in military history. Although there is little knowledge by those who perpetrated the criminal acts of the victims and of the objects, as it were - I don't mean it in a military sense - which were struck by the hundreds, perhaps up to a thousand projectiles, that came from JNA forces, the depravity of the act, the incredible recklessness interspersed with deliberate intent requires an examination of how such things could happen with career-military personnel the calibre of someone like Admiral Jokic. First, the images which are normally conjured up when one thinks of the shelling of the old town of Dubrovnik are images of buildings, of antiquity, of precious items being ruined. Of course, this is the case, but first and foremost we have to turn our attention to the fact that the old town of Dubrovnik was a living city, not a museum, and there were human beings whose lives were either ended or irrevocably altered by the events of the 6th of December, 1991. What happened? After approximately three months of occupation of the areas surrounding the city of Dubrovnik, of which the old town is a part, both sides, the JNA and the Croatian defenders, were about to come to terms for a comprehensive cease-fire agreement which would end hostilities, although not necessarily end occupation. The negotiators for the parties deserve special attention. Representing the JNA was Admiral Jokic; representing the Croatian side were three high-level Croatian cabinet ministers. This is noteworthy in that most negotiations were held with local negotiators. The importance of this particular cease-fire, with its comprehensive aspect, cannot be underestimated. It's central to bear in mind. One of the most essential aspects of the cease-fire which the Admiral had been involved in negotiating was the restoration of basic necessary commodity, such as electricity and water, for the population of Dubrovnik. The only glitch which did not permit, in the Admiral's judgement, allowing the signature on the page, as of the 5th of December, was an issue about inspection of vessels. Dubrovnik was besieged in the sense of encirclement with a blockade of its port and surrounded from all sides by forces under the control of the JNA. In order to work out this particular detail, the Admiral indicated he would need to confer with persons higher than he in Belgrade. However, it was clearly understood by both sides that the cease-fire was effectively a done deal and would simply be consummated formally the next day, the 6th of December. Parties left with this understanding. Orders were passed down. And all sides -- both sides were to have been ready for the terms to have been implemented upon the working out of that last detail. What happened, however, on the very early morning hours of the 6th of December was not an implementation of the cease-fire but, rather, an unauthorised attack, as the evidence suggests, by forces under the control of Admiral Jokic but not ordered by Admiral Jokic. The attack was from forces in the area of Zarkovica, which is the Croatian stronghold -- I'm sorry, the JNA stronghold in the high ground on Srdj, the Croatian high ground stronghold. The chaos which ensued from this unauthorised attack, at least unauthorised from the perspective of Admiral Jokic, was that a full-blown fire-fight ensued. Simultaneously or almost simultaneously with the attack on the Croatian defenders at Srdj was the opening of fire on the old town of Dubrovnik. I would like to take a moment and just allow a visual assist to see, if I may, a little bit about the layout of Dubrovnik. If I can ask my colleague to produce Dubrovnik general view 5 first on Sanction, which is the mode of presentation for all our visual aids. If I can be sure that everyone has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, do you also have on your screen the picture just announced?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] .

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In order to acquaint the Chamber with the layout of the old town, it is the promontory which is pictured in the centre of the image. It is clearly surrounded by water on both sides. And behind it, in the next shot, which I would ask my colleague to proceed to, Your Honours can see that behind it are the high grounds. If we may proceed to yet the next photo, and the next, please; and the next, please. The Chamber should have a fairly good picture of the bird's-eye view from the high ground to the old town of Dubrovnik. The lovely barrel-tile roofs that you see on the promontory are the structures within the ancient walls of the old town of Dubrovnik. When I mentioned a few moments ago that fire was opened from Zarkovica, I would ask now to present a picture of what the old town looks like from Zarkovica, which was the JNA high ground stronghold. Sorry. We'll go back one. This would be one angle -- can we return, please. One who looks down from there, it has been said, can see coffee being drunk on the central dividing street of the old town, called the Stradun. I don't know if we'll be able to retrieve the particular photo -- I believe it is now -- is that correct? -- it is now in front of Your Honours. This is one of several views to indicate what it looked like to officers of the JNA. If I can ask you then to show the next view. Among the ordnance used from the high ground just pictured is a weapon called a Maljutka, which is a wire-guided missile, a precision instrument. Weapons of this type were directed against the old town and in fact detonated there, along with mortars and other forms of artillery. How did this come to pass? How did it happen that what should have been a cease-fire ended up in mayhem? There have been outstanding standing orders, directives, and other transmissions from the highest level of the Federal Yugoslav authorities as well as from Admiral Jokic and General Strugar that the -- his co-accused -- that the old town of Dubrovnik was not to be damaged, destroyed, attacked, or in any way molested. Despite the standing order, which has -- based in reason its cultural value, which is protected under the protocols of the Geneva Conventions and which is further evidenced by the UNESCO designation of world heritage site, which was granted to the old town of Dubrovnik, everything inside, including the walls, in 1979, no harm was to befall this demilitarised area. Nevertheless, in October of 1991 circumstances surrounding shelling incidents were not investigated when the old town was in fact engaged by mortar. Despite the standing order -- and I must repeat that it is not suggested now that in October the particular units involved were under the direct control of Admiral Jokic. However, in area of responsibility it was clearly known that there was an engagement of the old town, it was communicated through internationals to the JNA officer at the command level, yet nothing was done about it. A standing order as serious as that was allowed to be violated with impunity. The message: It's okay. Moving on to the month of November, some of the most aggressive shelling of the old town - not a stray round here, a stray round here, but aggressive, deliberate shelling of the old town occurred. Again, at this point in time involvement of units under the control of Admiral Jokic comes into play. What happens? No discipline, nothing. A stronger message: It may be on paper, it may be an order, but it's okay if you violate it. The type of climate that was allowed to grow and dominate from the command of the 2nd Operational Group, which included the 9th Naval Sector, which was Admiral Jokic's command, fostered a disregard, a disrespect, and a permissible violation of certain orders with impunity. The message: It's okay. Had a trial ensued, there would have been evidence presented of the nature of the sustained attack against the old town of Dubrovnik. I would suffice it to say that that is not part of the charge here; what is significant is that there was an awareness of the attack and nothing was done. We fast-forward now to the 5th of December, where after this long period of hostility and occupation surrounding the area is wearing down, certainly, the JNA forces. The cease-fire should be brought into play. The importance of this particular event, as I have indicated to Your Honours, evidenced in part by the level of negotiation - that is, cabinet level from the Croatian side; Admiral Jokic from the JNA side - required that every eventuality should be foreseen, that nothing disrupt it. That would include making sure that any units which had been problematic in the past that could cause any possible disruption would be appropriately handled in the context of command. That did not happen. Units that had been involved in shelling of the old town before again engaged in the same activity. This time, however, the consequences were much more long standing and the duration of the assault went from the early morning hours until late in the day on the 6th of December. I would like to ask, if I could, to show a -- an image of just some of the weaponry. This is the type of weaponry that was at the disposal of the forces of the JNA, along with the wire-guided missile and the mortars that we have -- that we have described. And the use of them or abuse of them is firmly a matter that is subject to regulation by the commanding officers. What appears to have happened, according to the evidence, is that once the assault was so intense there was no introduction of any immediate order to protect, to preserve the old town, which by necessity would have certainly been implicated in any of the assault arising from this unauthorised attack by the forces under Admiral Jokic. The Prosecution submits, and the Defence has so agreed, that there is a causal, direct causal connection between the failure to impose the required discipline of previous incidents of shelling an old town in direct violation of orders and the incident of unlawful attack against the old town on the 6th of December. The failure of command was such that it aided and abetted what happened on the 6th. It was a foreseeable consequence of all that had happened. And the actual consequences were simply disastrous. Again, the best predictor of future behaviour is past behaviour, and it was absolutely foreseeable that this could happen, and sadly it did. In this indictment which has been amended, the Chamber is aware that there were two civilian deaths and three injuries. Perhaps the numbers seem small, but the area is small, and every life lost or injured is a major -- has a major consequence, not only for families but because they are lives. It is significant also to have a look, if I may, at what has been described as a dispersal map of projectiles which impacted in the old town on the 6th of December. I believe -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It will be presented in Sanction, but if it would assist the Chamber to have a hard copy of it, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, we have seen a couple of photographs until now. Do we get hard copies of those shown to us? Because from what I've seen on my screen, there might be a huge number of photographs, but that those shown to the Chamber will be clearly identified so have at least one hard copy to be given to the registrar so that we know what selection you've made and what we've seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The hard copies have been made and they will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The points of impact are shown, and it is evident that very few areas in the old town were spared. I will attempt to give the Chamber in the time allotted to me a bit of a walk-through of the old town to see what happened on the 6th of December, and then I will return to the issue of the Admiral's role in it. If we can proceed, please, to show a series of historical photos from the date. This is an example from the date of a shell exploding in the old town of Dubrovnik. If we can move on, please, to the next. Again, engaging the old town. Next, please; the old town ablaze. Next, please. Next please. Next, please. Next. Next. One more, please. We are now going to move briefly through some of the examples of the destruction of property violative of Article 3, also, of the Statute. I will not narrate, but it is clear that the shelling damage has hit the cupola of this particular religious monument. Can we have the next photo, please. The inside of a structure. Next, please; no object appeared to have been spared. The amount of roof damage was quite significant, and of course the tiles were unique to Dubrovnik. And although repair has been possible, which we will show the Chamber, true restoration is difficult because of the nature of the structures, the materials that went into them, their age. Next, please. Craters which were memorialised. The actual walls of the city were also impacted; although, their strength is evident. It should be emphasised that the -- some of the weaponry used, particularly mortars, are designed to kill people, will not destroy buildings. They will be incendiary in their result and they will kill people, but the use of them here was simply criminal. Okay. If I can show some of the roof crater damage -- I'm sorry, the roof damage. The Onofrio fountain, a very well-known cultural object in the old town, suffered damage. And again, if the Chamber, when it has an opportunity to look carefully at the dispersal, will see that very few areas were spared. If I can try -- I realise that Sanction has its slowness right now, but if I can move on to a couple of points. If we could move to the last -- these shots, if it's possible. I would then move in briefly to discussing -- these are some of the shots, the last shots taken by one of the deceased victims, Pave Urban. And there is a volume that has been published in memoriam of his last shots taken prior to his Delta. He was a young journalist who had returned to Dubrovnik to document the destruction to the buildings in his city. Returning now to what Admiral Jokic did do after this broke out and continued. Although called to Belgrade to respond, the Admiral displayed an unusual expression of responsibility at the time, right at the time of the incident, realising that it should not have happened. The Admiral notified both the Croatians and the internationals and expressed regret at the time, indicating that it was not an ordered attack and that there -- he would be requesting an investigation. The ability to resume negotiations that same day was, of course, limited, but the Admiral directed his attention, his energies, to trying to get the process back on track for the cease-fire to come into effect. But, of course, bringing to a halt the type of action that broke out on the 6th of December was not a process that was quickly accomplished, certainly not a result that was quickly accomplished. On the 7th, the next day, the negotiations did resume. There will be -- it will be -- I'm sure the Defence will perhaps pre-empt the same commentary I'm about to make, but it is clear that the Admiral put his energies into making sure that the cease-fire that he had an interest in assuring to be implemented was signed and implemented. The conduct of the Admiral that day has been made known to the Office of the Prosecutor, whereby it has been said that Admiral Jokic was sincere in his efforts; the negotiators were willing to resume negotiation with him, despite the incredible disaster of the day before; and the process did come to its conclusion. At the end of it all, hundreds of structures were damaged. At the end of it all, two people died; an 18-year-old boy, young man, Mr. Tonci Skocko, and 23-year-old Pave Urban, lost their lives. Three persons were injured. And I will speak of them a bit later when I have a charge to do the victim impact. It would be very difficult to give a proper eulogy this many years later, but it would certainly be required that the Chamber know something about these individuals, and I will so present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, if I may interrupt you just for the order of this hearing. It was indicated to me that you would need approximately 35 minutes. Looking at the clock, you used 30 minutes until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you announced what is still to be said. So may I ask you to try to -- because we'd like to follow a tight schedule. May I ask you to keep an eye on the clock as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just -- I wanted to make sure that I understood clearly that I would have a chance to get back into the victim impact subsequent, because this is effectively what I was told was the opening part to give the context to the plea and the understanding of the event. So I will simply begin to conclude the opening remarks by indicating that despite what happened on the 6th, despite the incredibly serious nature of these unauthorised and unlawful attacks, no one was effectively disciplined from Belgrade; certainly not even the Admiral was disciplined. The atmosphere of impunity continued. The Admiral did require an investigation within his command to be undertaken. There was evidence that some action was taken, but insufficient to have yet again shown how seriously this should have been taken and really too late. No one suffered a loss of rank. Some were promoted. The Admiral, however, it should be indicated, was involuntarily retired in May of 1992. It is not difficult to conclude now, I hope for you, how this could have happened when the atmosphere, the climate of command was such that, effectively, anything went. Commanders whose troops, whose subordinate units are charged with operating weapons are responsible for what happens with those weapons. Judgement, reasonableness must govern. The underlying issue here was the absence of any actual sense of control over troops who had gone wild before and were to have repeated their actions. A comment about the recommendation of sentence, which I will really discuss at the closing point of the hearing today: The Prosecution had recommended a cap of ten years as the appropriate sentence, in the absence of any mitigating factors. I submit to the Chamber that there are substantial mitigating factors in this case, and they have been outlined in the brief submitted by the Prosecution. And I'm sure that the Defence has also -- plans also to make it clear what they are. It is significant that Admiral Jokic is the highest-ranking officer of what was the JNA to have pled guilty. It is, in my view, more significant that at the time of the event he recognised the fundamental wrong of the incident. And whatever ensued -- and again, the criminality of it is absolutely patent, but it is a very complex set of circumstances that seem to have prevailed in the command of the entire Dubrovnik campaign, and this was one of the tragic consequences of the failure of command of that entire campaign, and in particular, as regards units that had access to weapons that could be directed and were directed against the old town. The fact of the plea is very significant for reconciliation. A man of the admiral's background and level, rank, effectively holding himself before this Chamber and indicating that he accepts responsibility for acts of his subordinates, which is the essence of command responsibility, is a -- a factor that I think is very significant to bear in mind throughout this entire presentation. I thank you for your attention on this point, and I will return at a later point to give more Prosecution evidence -- input.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Nikolic, I did understand that the Defence would need far shorter for its introductory -- its opening remarks in respect of sentencing. It was indicated to me that it would take some five minutes. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN

My learned friend from the Prosecution has set out for us the context which brings us here today. I intend to address you at length at the close of proceedings today during my final oral submissions. For now let me say that the Defence intends to call two witnesses during this hearing. First you will hear from retired rear admiral Pogacnik. Mr. Pogacnik and Admiral Jokic have known each other professionally and personally for over 20 years. Mr. Pogacnik was deputy commander to Admiral Jokic in the 9th Naval Sector in the mid-1980s. Mr. Pogacnik will testify about Admiral Jokic's career in the navy, his knowledge of Admiral Jokic's political and social views, and the circumstances which brought Admiral Jokic to Dubrovnik in October 1991. The second Defence witness is Mr. Miroslav Stefanovic, a founding member of the political party New Democracy. He will testify concerning Admiral Jokic's political activities in Serbia in the 1990s and in particular the significant contribution Admiral Jokic made to the development of the New Democracy initiative for having FRY join Partnership for Peace. And finally, Mr. President, Admiral Jokic himself will address the Trial Chamber. And, Mr. President, those are my opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. If you'd just give me one second for -- to confer with Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the most tragic part of the entire unfortunate incident is the loss of life and the damage to the lives of those who survived, either as loved ones or as injured victims. And I would take at this time an opportunity, albeit a number of years later, to have the privilege to tell the Chamber something about the persons whose names appear in the indictment, the amended indictment, so that they can understand who these people, these human beings were. I would ask, if I may, first start by age. And I want just to clarify to the Chamber in a pre-trial -- or a 65 ter Conference we indicated that we would request your indulgence to transpose the dates of birth shown in the indictment for the two deceased victims. And we will start with a bit of background about a young person named Tonci Skocko. Tonci Skocko, a young civilian male, was only 18 years old at the time of his violent death from the human beings were. I would ask, if I may, first start by age. And I want just to clarify to the Chamber in a pre-trial -- or a 65 ter Conference we indicated that we would request your indulgence to transpose the dates of birth shown in the indictment for the two deceased victims. And we will start with a bit of background about a young person named Tonci Skocko. Tonci Skocko, a young civilian male, was only 18 years old at the time of his violent death from the shelling shrapnel on the 6th of December in the old town of Dubrovnik. Son of Mato, who has provided some insight into his son. He had aspirations to do many things which, of course, were cut short in the prime of his life. What happened was he was struck by lethal shrapnel as he ran back -- I'm sorry, as he had come outside of his father's grocery store, which was situated in the old town. He was in the company of another person who was injured, a person named Nikola Jovic, who is listed also as one of the injured parties in the amended indictment. The shrapnel, according to the medical examiner's report, pierced his chest and heart, and he died as a direct consequence of those wounds. The photo has been provided by the family, and I am hopeful that he -- his family understands that the interests are represented by this representation -- by this particular photo representation. I'll wait till it's distributed to the usher, if I may. The second deceased victim mentioned in the second amended indictment was an individual named Pave Urban, 23 years old at the time of his violent death from shrapnel injuries. There is a bit more that has been made known about his young life to the public because of his passion for photography. We have heard from his mother, who shall also appear as part of a video, which I will ask the Chamber to view, that her son was killed doing what he loved to do most, which was taking pictures. He was in the old town trying to capture for posterity the images of the vicious assault by the JNA forces and although at a distance, was hit by shrapnel that took his life. We were able to gather a little bit of information about the circumstances through a friend, a Mr. Ivo Djuric -- I'm sorry, Djuro Ivic, I beg your pardon, who was looking out the window of his apartment, and saw his friend, a journalist and photographer, Pave Urban, hit by a shell. He said he was hit at some distance, about 20 metres from the location where Mr. Ivic was, fell down, lay on his stomach, and after a time, although he was taken away by the ambulance, it appeared that he was lifeless and succumbed to his injuries then and there. As I have mentioned earlier, in the photo you see placed on your screens is a photo of Pave Urban. A memorial album has been released which has the last shots taken prior to the death of Mr. Urban and is touching, poignant, and perhaps portrays more than my words can ever say about what was happening in the old town on that fateful day. I will move now to the persons who suffered injury. I have been provided photographs of these individuals so that you can see a little bit for yourselves. The first individual is Mr. Vlasica - is that correct? - okay. And Mr. -- if I may tell you a bit about him. Ivo Vlasica, son of Ivanko, Marijana. Father of two, was 35 years old - three-five - years old on 6 December 1991. As a civilian, he had been working in a shop in the old town and was standing in the doorway of the shop. A shell exploded some 7 metres away, detonating on the terrace of a restaurant located at an angle from the shop. Because the old town is constructed as it is, an ancient town, its lanes are narrow and they are so narrow that shrapnel can ricochet back and forth between the walls of the old town. Bearing in mind that the old town is a living city full of people, residents, shop-keepers, the ricochetting shrapnel struck Mr. Vlasenica, going through his upper right leg with smaller pieces of shrapnel, hitting his feet and arms. The next person is Mr. Mato Valjalo. Mr. Valjalo was born 18 May 1948. And on the 6th of December he was heading toward city hall along the main street, the main dividing avenue of Dubrovnik called the Stradun. He heard a shell hit behind him. He fell to the ground, lost consciousness, and when he regained consciousness found himself covered in blood, having observed pieces of shrapnel in his legs and arms and also having realised he suffered serious head injuries. Mr. Valjalo is a husband and a father of two daughters. I regret that I do not have a photograph of Nikola Jovic, but I would like to be able to tell the Chamber something about him. Mr. Jovic, who was also injured during the shelling of the 6th, was injured in the same incident which resulted in the death of Tonci Skocko. Mr. Jovic was working in the shop of Mato Skocko, the father of Tonci Skocko, when the projectile detonated in the shrapnel hit Tonci and hit himself. His injuries were to the area of the chin and leg. He describes the shock, the shock that one senses and feels when confronted with this type of event, the horror of shrapnel, the horror of shelling. These are the human losses, and of course there's nothing that can be said further to bring these people back. We hope that their deaths are not in vain and that they are remembered by all who understand the futility of the action that happened in Dubrovnik that day. If I may turn for a moment to a video which we think will best portray the losses, the damage, the injury, as it were, to the living monuments, the objects, to Dubrovnik as an ancient, protected city. It would be, I think, more effective for Your Honours to see than for me to further narrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed to show the video to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: NARRATOR: -- north or the south, from east or west, she is never anything less than a finely balanced result of the work of both man's hand and his irrepressible spirit, tenacity, ingenuity, an imperative instinct for survival, wisdom and perseverance; all these have coalesced those, the dividing line, between two quite distinct civilisations. Through the long centuries, while other Croatian lands formed part of other states the skill of Dubrovnik's diplomats and the impregnability of its fortifications, guaranteed its independence and freedom and that it remained a republic of high international stand, both as a commercial power and as a significant maritime force. Many of Dubrovnik's citizens won world renown and world-famous artists travel to the city to enhance it still further through their industry and their works. Dubrovnik is a monument city. Its medieval structure which grew out of the principles of the statute of 1272 have been preserved to this day. The focal point of it legal and administrative power, the seat of government, was the Ducal Palace. Another palatial building, Sponza the palace, once the State Mint and Customs and Excise office, today house it is city's historical archives, one of the richest of its kind in the whole of the Mediterranean. The ancient pharmacy in Dubrovnik was among the earliest to be established anywhere in Europe. All this is lovingly protected by the city's patron saint, St. Blasius, whose statues are to be seen on the city gates, on its walls, fortresses and other public buildings. Relics of the much-revered saint are housed in the cathedral's treasury. In 1979, Dubrovnik, its priceless beauty, and the state of preservation of the city's monuments, was designated a world heritage site by UNESCO. Its singular beauty and charm has made Dubrovnik one of the best-known tourist destinations in the world, the traditional summer festival being one of its attractions. It is said that streets with the elegance and allure of Dubrovnik's Stradun, the city's main thoroughfare, are to be seldom seen anywhere. This mirror of stone lives on through humanity's touch, through man's tread and his laughter. It abandons its to the casual stroller. During the most devastating attack on December 6th, 1991, something like 1.000 shells rained down on the old town within its walls and in the immediate vicinity. At the end of 1991, Dubrovnik was listed as an endangered world heritage site by UNESCO. Spring has burgeoned once more. It is now 1995, and Dubrovnik is displaying its normal image. Details show that restoration work is underway. The city's clock tower shows the correct time, as usual. The cupola and the section of the stone tower which suffered direct hits have now been repaired. The roof of the Sponza palace have been restored and people are again able to use the flight of stairs called uzjezuits [phoen] or "alongside the Jesuits." The old well in the convent of St. Clare's Cloisters as well as a major part of the roof have also been restored. No longer is there a gaping hole to attack from the beauty of the great Onofrio fountain. Damaged sections of the stone balustrade of the bridge at Pula have been replaced. During the shelling of Dubrovnik, 111 projectiles pounded Europe's-best preserved fortification systems. Today those magnificent walls have for the most part been repaired and sections are once again open to visitors. Disruption and serious damage was also inflicted on the Franciscan monastery and the Church of Friars Minor. To date the bell tower, the staircase leading to the entrance, and a section of the roof have undergone repair. Work on the roofs of the Dominican monastery in St. Dominic's church have been completed. The large cross that had once stood for centuries above the main altar had to be removed for reasons of safety. Repairs have been carried out to the roof of the synagogue. The small Church of Sigurate, badly damaged by direct hits, also has also been restored following lengthy and detailed research. Part of the roof, gable and bead moulding of the roof of St. Joseph have also been repaired. The colour of the stone of the balustrade and the medallion of the Church of St. Blasius betray their renovation. Only time will mellow the varying nuances presently visible on the facade, the roof and the staircase. The chapel of the sacred heart located within Djordjik Minory [phoen] Palace has now been restored. During the worst of the shelling which occurred on December the 6th, 1991, was palace of the Dubrovnik festival at No. 1, Od Sigurate Street, was seriously damaged by fire. So far the site has been cleared and the roof replaced. Medallions on the first floor have been protected while work on the damaged stucco has revealed war murals dating from early periods. Repairs to residential buildings began even while Dubrovnik was still under siege. In the city's old core, about 70 per cent of roofs suffered direct hits. As a result of systematic restoration, more than half the damage has now been put to rights. The restoration and revitalisation of a town is not merely a construction enterprise. It is, in fact, the subtle art of adjusting historical entity to modern-day life, taking it step by step to ensure the preservation of its authenticity. It is first and foremost the enhancement of both the quality of life of the town and in the town. At the same time, it is the repayment of our debt to the past, which is bequeathed us so much wealth, and a sacred obligation to pass it on enriched by our own efforts and our own times to future generations; for them to pass it on, and then on again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that is the conclusion of the video, and that concludes the section on victim impact by the Prosecution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. The Defence would like first to call witnesses, as I do understand. Can these witnesses be examined in open session, or is there any need to go into private or closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, they can be heard in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then suggest, also looking at the clock, it was scheduled I think your first witness for some 40 minutes; is that correct? For some 40 minutes. That would bring us close to 1.00. And I would like to spend a few minutes, perhaps the last few minutes before the break, to give an opportunity to the parties to submit whatever they want to submit in respect of a request for a continued provisional release. So therefore, Mr. Nikolic, if you're ready to call your first witness. I did understand from the 65 ter meeting that last week the statement of the second witness was not yet read by the Prosecution. I take it that meanwhile the statement has been provided so that the Prosecution could prepare for the second witness. And at that time, it was expected that there would be no cross-examination. After having read the statement of the second witness, has this changed, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Based on what was written, no, Your Honour. And we'll see if it comports with what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Well, Mr. Nikolic, you may call your first witness, and that will be ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marjan Pogacnik. Your Honours, I would like to request assistance if possible, if I could have this plastic pulpit for the papers to be moved from the Prosecution desk to our disk here because we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a shared asset between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you escorted already the first witness. And that's fine. No -- please. Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to notify you that Ms. Jelena Nikolic will be questioning our first witness, Mr. Marjan Pogacnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pogacnik, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text has been handed out in your own language to you by the usher. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Pogacnik. You'll first be examined by Ms. Jelena Nikolic, Defence counsel. The Defence has called you as a witness. Please proceed, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Ms. Nikolic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Pogacnik. Could you please tell your name?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: My name is Marjan Pogacnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court where you were born and when.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: I was born in Ljubljana in 1941.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether you speak, read, and write the Serb and Croatian language well --

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- bearing in mind the fact that you are of Slovenian ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I read, write, and speak it well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can then provide your answers in that language.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about your education after the elementary and secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: After I graduated from the secondary school in Ljubljana, I studied at the Naval Academy in Divulje. After I graduated from the naval military academy, I specialised for submarine service. And then after 1973 until 1976. I graduated from the command and Staff College in Belgrade. And then in 1979 and 1980 I graduated from the command and staff school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1985, to which post were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: In 1975, in July, as a naval officer I was appointed to the post of the chief of staff. At the same time I was the deputy commander of the 9th Naval Sector in Boka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. The question in translation was about 1985. The answer in translation - I'm not saying that the original answer was the same - was about 1975. Could you please clarify whether we have a translation problem or whether there's a misunderstanding between you, Ms. Nikolic, and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try. [Interpretation] I will try to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In my question, Mr. Pogacnik, I referred to 1985 in July. In fact, my question referred to 1975 and now I want to clarify whether it's 1985 or 1975.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: It was in 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the same class at the Naval Academy as Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: No. I was five years younger, which means that Mr. Jokic was the ninth class and I was the fourteenth class in the Naval Academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how do you know Mr. Jokic, since when.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Jokic since our -- my graduation from the academy. I got to know him better when we came to the naval port of Lora as submarine officers where we took part in submarine exercises in the islands around Split and Vis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start seeing him more often, and in fact to cooperate with him as a officer?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: We started seeing each other more often in the 1980s, when I, as the commander of a submarine unit, cooperated with Mr. Jokic to improve the submarine service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Jokic was first appointed the commander of the 9th Naval Sector in Boka?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: I do know it quite well, and I remember that he was appointed in 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know until when he remained in that post?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: He remained there until 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were appointed in 1985 the chief of staff of the 9th Naval Sector in Boka.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period, you were in daily contact with Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was your commander at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, he received me in his capacity as the commander, and until my -- the time when I left the naval sector in Boka we were in daily contact during the working hours and, if necessary, also in our free time. We were in constant contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what terms -- in fact, what was your relationship like with Mr. Jokic, in view of the fact that you were the chief of staff and he was the commander of the naval sector at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that in his capacity as a commander he welcomed me there, he helped me in the first six months to learn the ropes of the chief of staff and his deputy. And when he realised that I did learn my craft, he started training me for the post of the commander of the naval sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the career of Mr. Jokic as a naval officer? And if yes, how come?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite familiar with it. When I became a young officer, he was already well known as an excellent officer. Whenever he was a commander, that unit was always the best, first a commander of a torpedo boat or a patrol boat. And then he was also a commander of a destroyer in Split. He was an example for all of us young officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Mr. Jokic treated his subordinate officers and his superiors?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. He was, first of all, very humane. He was a very professional soldier. He asked his subordinates to show full responsibility, but he also showed understanding for any problems, not only as an officer regarding his subordinates but he also inquired about their families. He was interested in their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were very often in contact with him in those days, are you familiar with the political views of Mr. Jokic in late 1980s and early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes. He was always of a Yugoslav orientation. He was always opposed to any improper behaviour. He was always for full equality of all nations and ethnic groups. That was his main point, what he really believed in. He never expressed any nationalist views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the 1990s, there was the one-party system in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. Could you please tell us what this party was and were you, as officers, members of this party?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, that was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. And all of us officers in the Yugoslav People's Army, as of 1969, were in fact forced to become members of that party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at a congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia in late 1990 in a delegation together with Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Although I was never involved in politics, I always held command posts. At that time, I was elected by my sector at the time, which was in Pula, to act as a delegate at the well-known 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, where I met Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia important?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Well, at the 14th Congress, Yugoslavia began to break up. And in fact, the League of Communists stopped functioning after the 14th Congress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the Yugoslav crisis in the party was the topic of the congress, what was the official standpoint of the JNA as regards the resolution of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: The official standpoint to have JNA was that Yugoslavia should be preserved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the standpoint reflected in the course of the 14th Congress?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: It turned out that the standpoint was not in fact correct because members of the delegation of the JNA voted the same way as the delegates of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the stand that you and Mr. Jokic supported and how did you vote at the 14th Congress?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: We, as the only delegates from the delegation of the Yugoslav People's Army, voted differently from all the others. First of all, we voted in favour of the lifting of the economic blockade of the Republic of Slovenia, and we also voted in favour of the acceptance of the resolution on the confederal structuring of Yugoslavia. We did that because we saw that this was the only way to find a peaceful resolution for the crisis in Yugoslavia and for possible peaceful parting of ways of the Republics of the Yugoslav Federation, who would perhaps then form their own states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that your stand -- your and Mr. Jokic's stand was opposed to the warmongering policy which was already in the wings at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, we were absolutely opposed to any war. We were in favour of a peaceful way to part ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I would now like to go back to the 9th Naval Sector. Do you know who was the commander of the 9th Naval Sector in 1990 and in 1991, when hostilities had already begun in the area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: I know that very well. It was late Komodor Krsto Djurovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Komodor Krsto Djurovic, the late Komodor Krsto Djurovic?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes. We attended the academy at the same time. We knew each other from 1959 and we served in various submarines together for 15 years. We were friends and our families were also on good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Krsto Djurovic, the commander of the 9th Naval Sector in early October 1991; and how did you come to learn that?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: About this alleged helicopter accident -- the reason why I say "alleged" is because I never believed it was an accident -- I heard about it through the media and also from his relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear, that Mr. Djurovic had died?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, that he died in a helicopter accident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear later who was appointed the commander of the 9th Naval Sector a few days after the death of Mr. Djurovic when the operations around Dubrovnik were in full swing already?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about that. I knew that Mr. Miodrag Jokic was appointed to that point again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a long-term officer and someone who knew the situation in the navy and one who knew the military sector in Boka and Mr. Jokic, what was your reaction when you heard that Vice-Admiral Jokic had taken over the duties -- had yet again taken over the duties of the 9th VPS, the 9th Naval District?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: I was really surprised for a number of reasons. First of all, as a commander of the VPS for many years, when he left that duty, he could have expected a position of far greater responsibility in the JNA. In my opinion, he was fit for a greater -- a more important position. I think that this was a means of demoting him. And when I asked myself why he had been appointed, I came to the conclusion that in fact they didn't have a more experienced high-ranking officer, since the commander who took those duties at that time was going to have an enormous and very responsible task. He was going to have to receive all the units and the equipment and institutions of the VPS at the time. That means the Pula naval sector, the Sibenik naval sector, the fleet, Vis, Lastovo and Losinj, which were naval strongholds; the academy, the hydrographic institute, et cetera. There were other institutions as well, enormous amounts of equipment, of ammunition and other technical means, not to mention the men and the families from all of those sectors. And Mr. Jokic had to provide these men and these families, had to make it possible for them to live a normal life, as they say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Judges what happened to the 5th Naval Sector and the 8th in autumn 1991. Why was the commander of the 9th VPS appointed these duties, apart from having other duties?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me explain what happened. In September, all those units were already getting prepared to leave the peacetime locations because of pressure from the outside, and especially in the case of Istria, which is an area I know well, they wanted to avoid fighting there. And Mr. Jokic, as commander of the 9th VPS, of the Boka VPS, which is where all those units and all that equipment were directed to, he was not just the commander, he was also a commander of that garrison and he was responsible for taking in these men, for deploying those units and for providing them with accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given that you have known Mr. Jokic for many years, can you tell us whether you know what Admiral Jokic's family situation is.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mr. Jokic married and does he have any children?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic is married. He has two daughters. The names are Sanja and Tanja. All I can say that -- is that he always behaved in an exemplary manner as a father. He took care of his family. He brought them up very well. But I would say that he was always worried about the health of his youngest daughter above all, his younger -- youngest daughter was called Tanja.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Ms. Somers, is there any ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just one question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Admiral. How are you? Mr. Pogacnik, can you I understand if you've had prior meetings with the Office of the Prosecutor, prior meetings And I'll turn your attention back to, let's say, June of 2002. If you could indicate that, please.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes. I had contact in July of that year. I saw Ms. Somers in Ljubljana and Mr. Wiley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be Mr. Wiley? Is that the name you're referring to, Wiley?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Wiley. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, did you also indicate that based on your experience and knowledge you would be equally agreeable to rendering any assistance necessary to the Office of the Prosecutor if it were needed?

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pogacnik, I would have one question for you, that's the following: You told us about how you and Mr. Jokic voted at the 14th Congress of the Communist League. Were these votes public votes? Would you give your votes aloud or were these secret votes? Could you explain how the -- briefly how the voting procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MARJAN POGACNIK
utterances.text: This was a public vote. Every delegate received green and red card, and when it was time to vote the green card meant that the proposal was being accepted and the red one meant that it was being rejected. This was all very visible, especially in the part where the delegates in uniform were sitting. Now, we were immediately criticised afterwards on the spot, because we hadn't conducted ourselves in a disciplined manner, in accordance with what our representative in the Presidency of the Congress had expressed. It's because we had shown a card which was not identical to one that he had used. That's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Pogacnik. This, then, concludes your evidence in this sentencing hearing. I'd like to thank you for having come a -- from a long distance and having answered the questions of both the parties and the Bench. Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. You are excused, Mr. Pogacnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to first raise one procedural issue before we would turn into private session in order to discuss the provisional release issue. Ms. Somers, I noted that the Chamber has been provided with the statements of persons, for example, you referred to Mr. Ivic, who told us about Pave Urban. These statements are mainly redacted. Could you give us some clarification, first of all, on whether the Defence is aware of how they were redacted and also what is the specific reason for this redaction. Could you please address that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course, Your Honour. These statements were in fact redacted with the express consent and at the request of the Defence. The statements are broader than issues that would concern this particular second amended indictment, and in the interests of justice, we wanted to narrow and focus them. Accordingly, all redaction was done literally sitting with the Defence and with their full -- with mutual agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is that the other parts may have been relevant for other cases but it's mainly on the basis of relevance that you took out parts of it. I take it, since no one jumps up, that Ms. Somers has -- has expressed what is the view of the Defence? Yes. Having said that, I would like to turn into private session. And for the audience, I already indicate that once private session will be finished, we'll have a break for approximately 1 hour, and we'd like to resume, then, at 2.00, I think, but we first will deal with the issue of provisional release during a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the moment I think that the Defence could call its second witness. The second witness would be ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second witness, Your Honours, is Mr. Miroslav Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Stefanovic, I take it? Mr. Stefanovic, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you by the usher. And may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence has called you as a witness, and you'll be examined by Mr. Nikolic, Defence counsel for Mr. Jokic. Please proceed, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nikolic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zarko Nikolic. I'm the Defence counsel for Admiral Jokic, and I will be examining you for about 20 minutes. We have heard your name, but for the record I would like you to state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born, Mr. Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Lige [phoen] in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about your education.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of architecture in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that you are an architect, you have a degree in architecture.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, both you, Mr. Nikolic, and you, Mr. Stefanovic, since you're speaking the same language, if you do not make a small pause between question and answer, the interpreters will not be able to follow it and we might not hear your testimony, Mr. Stefanovic. So would you please keep that in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will make sure that I keep it in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So will I, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what did you do in your profession?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I mostly did designs of buildings and also construction of buildings, but also some infrastructure. I mean, interior design of buildings and also some really serious projects of infrastructure. This is mostly what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your work so far, have you received any awards?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received several awards at public competitions in architecture and also some other awards in my profession. So I can in fact perhaps boast a bit and state that I was quite successful in my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what is it that you do today? Where do you work? And what kind of work do you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I own a company that deals with engineering and design, which is named Kolubara, and it also has in its possession several other companies which also deal with designs, architectural design and construction work. I have a full-time job in the Assembly of the State Commonwealth of Serbia and Montenegro, but I still deal with architecture, and this is indeed my plan; I intend to do work in architecture until -- for the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your previous answer, it -- one could conclude that you are an active -- you have an active role in politics and in society.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of a political party? And if yes, which one?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I am the founding member of a party which was called New Democracy until March this year, and now it is called Liberals of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when was -- when was New Democracy founded?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us, when was the multi-party system introduced in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: It began officially in 1990, when parties were allowed to be registered. But to a certain extent we did have some attempts to launch the multiparty system as early as in 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apparently you got really interested in that process. You said that you were one of the founders of the New Democracy Party. Could you please tell us, what were the ideas and the platform of New Democracy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to be brief. I will just state two or three basic goals in our platform. First of all, it was a pronounced pro-European orientation of our party; we still abide by it. The second part has to do with the economy. Our approach is very liberal, emphasising the role of the market economy. And the third aspect, which is equally important, is human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, who were the members of New Democracy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were or who are members?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who are members?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the founders of New Democracy had two wings: The first was the Social Democratic Union of Youths, which in 1990 split from the Socialist Youth union - that was the reformist wing of the youth movement in Serbia. And the second part consisted of the rest of us, who were a bit older at the time. We wanted to achieve change, and we had some movements for cities, as we called them at that time, that propounded ideas that I just discussed with you. And together with those young people, we set up this party. First of all, the current Minister of Interior was there. He was the president at the time. Myself, a large number of people who are still members of the Liberals of Serbia party, but also a large number of people joined us later on. In 1992, then, that was when Mr. Jokic joined us officially. I say officially because there had been unofficial contacts between us before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point of my question was to indicate whether people who were members of New Democracy had a democratic bent.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Even more than that. Not only did they have a democratic bent, they also had a liberal bent. I have to stress once again the three segments: Pro-European orientation, our main goal being for us to become members, full members of the European Union, which is our final political goal in that respect; then also the economy which would be the same as the economy that exists in European Union, with the same conditions that exist there; and I also want to stress that right from the beginning we always paid a great deal of attention to human rights and the respect for human rights in Serbia and in the wider region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a representative of New Democracy, you were an assembly -- a deputy in the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, at the first free election -- well, conditionally speaking, free elections, as free as they could be at the time -- I was elected as a deputy in the Federal Assembly. In 1996, I was re-elected. In 1998, Mr. Milosevic -- in fact, it was in 1990, after the war, Milosevic took away my mandate because he forced the results. And then in the well-known September elections in 2000, when Milosevic's regime was toppled, I was re-elected a deputy. And this spring, when the Commonwealth of Serbia and Montenegro was set up, I was again elected as a deputy in the Assembly of the Commonwealth, and this is where I still am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I know Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known him for a long time by sight only, but as for any closer contact and cooperation with him, that began in 1992, when he became officially a member of New Democracy Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Admiral Jokic was a member of New Democracy Party.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was, and he was quite an active member of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Admiral Jokic was an active member of the party. Do you mean by that that he took part in the drafting and implementation of certain programmes of the party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's what I mean. And I can tell you what is it that Admiral Jokic had taken such an active part in. Admiral Jokic was the chairman of our board for defence and security. The board dealt with the issues that are self-evident from its name. And Admiral Jokic was one of the persons that -- in fact, he was perhaps the main propounder of the idea that our country should immediately, after the Partnership for Peace programme was set up, to join this programme and later on that it should join NATO. I believe that he really did a lot of work on that, trying to achieve that as the chairman of the board, and we discussed this issue at length. This would then be part of his activity. I believe that this was the most important part. And I hope that we will see it realised, at least as far as the Partnership for Peace programme is concerned, and I hope that we will not have to wait long until we join NATO. That was the first part. The second part concerned the reform of the military, which also was linked with the joining of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of Partnership for Peace and NATO, and also the reform of the police force. We all know what it was like in Milosevic's time. Admiral Jokic had quite radical ideas about the reform, both of the military and of the police force. According to me they were quite positive, and it would have been quite nice had these reforms been put into place, the reforms that Admiral Jokic and his group from the New Democracy had put forward. And I believe that had this happened, I believe that our country would have fared much better, our poor country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This initiative by the New Democracy Party, the Partnership for Peace programme, is it the consequence -- direct consequence of the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so. The official request was submitted immediately after the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords, but the discussions and talks that I mentioned earlier began immediately after the setting up of the Partnership for Peace. I believe it was in 1993 or 1994. So I wouldn't really make much of the connection between the Dayton Peace Accords and this initiative, although the Dayton Peace Accords gave us some kind of a hope that things would improve that it would be easier to achieve things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This initiative of yours to join the Partnership for Peace programme, did you want to push it through the Federal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I submitted a draft decision on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia joining the Partnership for Peace programme. It was on the 9th of January. And I have to state that I did write this text myself but it was done after lengthy discussions with Admiral Jokic and the board that he chaired. I think that the person behind the ideas expressed in this text is Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask that the draft decision be placed on the ELMO. I have copies of the original in B/C/S and of the English translation for the Bench and the registry and the Prosecution, and I would like to ask the registrar to give a number to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Nikolic. Madam Registrar, I do not know whether specific numbers will be given for sentencing purposes, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is possible, Your Honour, to give them a number for the sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think since we received also some photographs that finally numbers related to the sentencing hearing will be appropriately given to these documents. Yes, you may distribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like you to have a look at the document and tell us whether this is the draft decision that you spoke about a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is; that's the draft decision that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following question about this document, about this draft decision is: Can you briefly tell us whether this decision contained clear arguments as to why such a decision was essential for the state. Why it was essential to adopt such a decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the situation from our present situation, from this perspective, I think that this text, the first and second paragraph in this text, shows that it's very clear that at the time we realised that if we failed to change something in our state and in our policies, if we failed to change our way of thinking, the result would be certain terrible things, which unfortunately happened. Could I read out the first two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: "Our country and our people are at an important crossroads today. The selection -- the path that we select will determine our destiny for a very long period of time. It is now the right and unique moment to select a path that over the course of several decades will bring us to a state of welfare and not some new and perhaps even worse war. That, above all, requires a decision as to with whom we will proceed and as to where we will go and as to who our partners will be and who we will have mutual interests with."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we have given this document to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution, they will be able to read through the entire draft decision. Just one more thing about this document: Can you tell us, what happened to the draft decision in the Federal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the -- it's just like to say a few things about certain constitutional matters before I address that issue, some matters that are very important. A deputy had the right to suggest a law or a decision - a decision is more or less the same thing as a law - and in a certain period of time, a fairly short period of time probably, because I requested that this be dealt with as a matter of urgency, it was necessary to forward this to a chamber and the deputies had to discuss the decision. This draft decision, regardless of the fact that, as I said, it was a constitutional duty, never -- was never received by the Chamber, in spite of the fact that I and my party insisted on this happening. So by the 5th of October, 2000 it didn't -- it wasn't submitted to the chamber of the Yugoslav parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you - and if you did - did you present this draft decision for the Partnership for Peace to the public at large?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my party did this. It was done on several occasions through public discussions, but there were also some discussions about this in the media. We attempted to inform the public of this in the greatest possible detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At these discussions, when this decision was presented, did Admiral Jokic participate in these discussions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't just participate in these discussions. He was one of the main speakers and interpreters of this draft decision. He spoke about its importance, its meaning, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
