utterances.text: Could you single out a panel discussion in particular?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many of them there were exactly. The Admiral, Admiral Jokic probably knows. There were many of them in Serbia. But I would single out one that took place in February. I think it was the 27th of February, 1996, in the Belgrade Sava Centre, and a large number of ambassadors and military representatives from embassies participated in it, especially from the European Union countries and member states of the Partnership for Peace and members of the NATO pact. There were quite a lot of non-government organisation representatives. I think there were perhaps even over 50 participants in those discussions. I also remember that there was -- that the American and British ambassadors were present, as well as the Italian ambassador, the OSCE ambassador. But a lot of time has passed; I can't remember all of them. But there is a list of all the participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with this matter, would I be wrong to say that all the democratic forces in the world correctly understood the initiative of New Democracy, but the government in power at the time was not interested in such a democratic procedure at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you are correct. This was supported not only by the democratic forces in the country and in the world and by all people of goodwill, but as the government in Serbia and Yugoslavia didn't have any understanding for many other things, it didn't have any understanding for this matter either. Three years prior to this we had this terrible war, and unfortunately we were -- I think it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This initiative from the 1990s, did it become something that was discussed again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, immediately after the 5th of October, when Milosevic fell from power. We participated in this activity too, but there is a new proposal that we have submitted now. I think that part of our work that concerns the Partnership for Peace is something that we have completed in 1996, so we suggested that the Assembly should take a decision about entering NATO. That proposal didn't -- wasn't discussed by the Assembly either because at that Assembly we had the Socialist People's Party of Montenegro, which was a partner of the government. Such were the circumstances. It was a partner at the federal level, and they didn't allow this to go forward. For a certain period of time it was one of -- it was Mr. Milosevic's partner and they probably thought about things in the same manner. But in the meantime, when the joint state of Serbia and Montenegro was formed, the relationship of force between those two states was changed and the decision was proposed on joining the Partnership for Peace. I think this will be discussed in the future. Mr. Gobas [phoen], when he was in Montenegro, said that we would be received into this Partnership for Peace in May, when there was a meeting of the Partnership for Peace in Istanbul.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just show the witness this -- could this document be placed on the ELMO. I have a copy for the Trial Chamber and for the Prosecution and for the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please assist Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please answer briefly by saying yes or no. The text that you have before you, does it show that joining the Partnership for Peace is one of the priorities of the democratic powers right now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have also mentioned the year 1996. Was there anything that was characteristic of this year, anything important that happened in that year too?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes. That was the year in which elections for the Federal Assembly were held, as I have already said, and there were also the local elections for the assemblies of towns and municipalities. The Serbian Liberals -- or at the time, the New Democracy Party -- participated in those elections on its own, independently, not with any other groups. On one side you had the SBS and the JUL. After the elections, Slobodan Milosevic's regime falsified the results, and this resulted in large-scale demonstrations throughout Serbia, which finally resulted in the Council of European intervening. As far as I can remember, the former Spanish President appeared, Mr. Gonzales, I think, from the European Union or the European Council. And there were discussions according to which the real results should be accepted and at the time the opposition took over most of the towns in Serbia and we participated in some of -- in the government of some of the towns. The demonstrations were very important at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any direct information as to whether Admiral Jokic participated in those demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because at the time, Mr. Jokic became a little angry with us because, as I said, we participated in the elections on an independent basis and as a party we did not participate in those demonstrations because at the time we were in a coalition with the SPS, on the one side, and the republican government. But on the other side we participated on an independent basis in the elections, and this didn't cause us significant damage. Not many of our votes were stolen from us. And Admiral Jokic and other groups thought that we should participate in that as a party. We did condemn the falsification of the results, but we didn't take active participation in the demonstrations. But we did tell our members that they could participate in the demonstrations if they wanted to, and Mr. Jokic participated on a daily basis, as far as I know. But I would see him at these protest marches, as we called them, at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in September 2000 you became a federal deputy again, a deputy in the Federal Assembly. And with regard to this matter, do you know when the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that this -- passing this law caused a lot of trouble. It was adopted about -- in April 2002, about that time. The main problem, with regard to this law, was caused by one of our partners in the elections in 2000. It was Mr. Kostunica who caused the problems. He didn't want to vote for that law. And a more serious problem was that the party I have already mentioned, the Montenegro Party, the Socialist National Party, didn't want to vote for it; this was Mr. Bulatovic's party. So this law was just barely adopted in 2002, around April 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you find out that an indictment had been issued by The Hague Tribunal against Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. It was late autumn 2001. So it was sometime before the law was adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, it was 2001; October or November?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to lie, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at the time the law had not yet been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Mr. Jokic's decision to surrender was taken on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he decided to surrender on a voluntary basis. He alone took this decision. And I know this for certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stefanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Are there any questions by the Prosecution for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may ask just for one point of clarification which wasn't terribly evident. Perhaps it was just a -- a question of getting a date. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Stefanovic, when in 1992, the month in 1992, when the Admiral became part of your party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: But there are documents that show when this took place, documents that my party has. So it wouldn't be difficult to find out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can then just help me understand. Were there very many other high-ranking members or former members - depending on the month - of the JNA who were attracted to your party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two other high-ranking officers who entered the party, who joined the party, but that was a little later. Allow me to clarify something. In 1992, it was terrible -- in 2002, it was a terrible year for the opposition. We were an opposition party, and under the pressure of Slobodan Milosevic's regime. I want to emphasise this fact. Mr. Negovanovic and Dobrivojevic also joined. Those were the high-ranking officers who were also members and are still members of the Serbian Liberals. They were in the party too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, then, it was a relatively uncommon event for persons from the JNA to join your party. You were not speaking of vast numbers of former high-ranking JNA officers. So it's somewhat unusual to have this kind of membership in a very democratically oriented party; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was more than just a matter of personal courage if one was a member of a party which was pro-European, which was in favour of liberal economic policies and in favour of human rights. And in 1992, at that time, to become an active member of such a party, especially for high-ranking officers for the former JNA that, showed great personal courage in my opinion, and we were very content to see Mr. Jokic join us at the time. And he also accepted to be president of the committee and he represented us in public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, I would have one perhaps additional question to you perhaps related to the last question of Ms. Somers. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you do not exactly remember in what month in 1992 Mr. Jokic joined your movement or party. Do you remember whether he joined as still an active member of the armed forces or whether he was already out of function at that time? I mean, did you receive an active member of the forces or someone who had involuntarily retired?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember whether he was an active-duty serviceman at that time. But I do know that he did retire involuntarily; perhaps one could even say that he was punished. Had I known that you would be asking me such questions, I would have brought Mr. Jokic's admission certificate. But it shouldn't be a problem. This document could be submitted to the Court if it's necessary at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Necessary" is perhaps a big word. But if the parties could agree that there's any document which establishes the date of -- of membership, if there's any document. Of course, it -- it could be of some importance for the interpretation of the facts, because it might not be exactly the same whether you joined the party after involuntary retirement or -- I mean, causal relationships might go in different ways. I'm not saying that you could adduce that from those documents, but perhaps you could exclude some certain causal relationships by having dates. Could the parties agree on providing the Chamber with a document which would establish that date? Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, if it's convenient for the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then it's -- the Chamber would then accept such a document, even if provided after this sentencing hearing. And I take it that if that document, of which of course we might not even know what it looks like -- if there would be any comment to be given on, I would say that both parties can write down their comments on the document. For example, if it say that is it was in 1957, it certainly must be a mistake; so whatever comment. And the Chamber would like not to receive that document and any additional comment until both parties have showed to each other what comment they would like to make on that document. Is that clear enough as guidance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Stefanovic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you for having answered all questions, questions of the parties, also the questions of the Bench. I'd like to thank you for having come that far way to The Hague. You're excused. Mr. Usher, you could escort Mr. Stefanovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the Chamber apologises for conferring for a short while. Did I understand well that this would be the moment where Mr. Jokic would like to make a statement, which would be an unsworn statement although under the control of the Chamber? And I take it that you have explained to Mr. Jokic that it's up for the Chamber to assess whether this statement would have any probative value, even if we are talking about sentencing rather than about convictions; nevertheless, the probative value will be assessed by the Chamber. I take it that you've discussed this with Mr. Jokic, and that you, Mr. Jokic, do fully understand what your position is at this moment. I add to that that no questions can be put by the Prosecution in respect of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is all correct, and I will not be repeating what I have already said. I just wanted to propose at this moment that you give the floor to Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I thought it my duty to at least clarify once and forever the procedural situation. Mr. Jokic, you have an opportunity now to make a statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, Madam Prosecutor, I would like to thank you for giving me this opportunity to address you. Two years ago, immediately after the indictment was made public, I surrendered to the organs of the Tribunal in order to face the allegations and for the truth to come out. At that time, in my state, there was no legal framework for the cooperation with the Tribunal. None of the officers against whom indictments had been issued had not surrendered, and the public opinion was against such an act. Together with my Defence team and with the minimal assistance provided by the organs of the state and of the military, I thoroughly investigated and examined the allegations in the indictment and my individual and objective responsibility. I was aware of my command responsibility for the acts of my subordinates in combat and for the failings and mistakes in the exercise of command over troops. At the same time, I felt the need for us as a responsible society to openly and sincerely face the war crimes that have been committed. I believed that it was important to start cooperating with the Tribunal and that despite all the opposition and lack of understanding in the public somebody should definitely start the process of accepting the responsibility of asking forgiveness of the victims and, as the final goal, of achieving reconciliation with the environment. Your Honour, there are two reasons why I'm here today: The first is my personal conviction that as a commander I have a moral and personal obligation to accept responsibility and to ask forgiveness for the acts of my subordinates, even though I did not order them; the second reason is the awareness of the fact that my admission of guilt and repentance and remorse are more important than my personal fate. On the 6th of December, 1991, two people were killed, three people were wounded and substantial damage was caused to civilian structures and to cultural and historical monuments in the old town of Dubrovnik. The fact that these lives were lost in the area for which I was responsible will remain etched in my consciousness for the rest of my life. I am ready to bow before all the victims of this conflict, regardless of the side they were on, with the dignity of a soldier. Furthermore, although I had already done that in the course of the shelling itself over the radio, and afterwards I did it again in person, I feel the obligation to express my deepest sympathy to the families of those who were killed and wounded and the citizens of Dubrovnik for the pain and all the damage that was caused to them by the unit under my command. I see my regret as a prerequisite for reconciliation and the coexistence of various peoples in this area. Your Honour, I have been a professional soldier my whole life. As such, I have abided by the officers code trying to serve my profession and my country honourably. That is why I stand here before you, in hope that my act will contribute to the final reconciliation and that it will enable the people in this area to live together and that it will also create a possibility for my people not to bear the burden of guilt now and in the future. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokic. We will continue now with the closing arguments of the parties on sentencing. Ms. Somers, the Prosecution, the first party to give its views.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I would like to again direct Your Honours' attention to the very important contents of a statement, the second statement, to which we have made reference from September of this past year and strongly recommend that its contents be looked at. I think it will provide insight into events, insight into persons, and I think particularly insight into the thinking, then and now, of Admiral Jokic. Moving on. It is clear, of course, under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that the gravity of the offence is the principal consideration in sentencing. We have made it clear that of course the gravity of the consequences of unlawful attack are great in the -- with the resulting deaths and injuries and widespread destruction. We have also tried to do that which is not always easy, which is to assess whether everything that was believed to be correct in the Prosecution's theory was correct, and it has not been necessarily an easy road. Admiral Jokic has made that road clearer. Our job is to get to the truth, and it has been a process of getting to the truth, or at least a much better understanding of what really happened that has perhaps been one of the best by-products of this entire process, which of course is not a happy process for anyone. The absolute senselessness of the attack on the 6th of December defies comment. It stands by itself. The Admiral has acknowledged the same. There is no justification for it, not from him, really not from anyone who has an understanding of what was to have happened that day really and what happened ultimately. It is very important to try to look at sentencing practices, in the eyes of the Prosecution, not so much from the objective possibilities of what one could end up with, as it were, but sentencing as a very personalised process. One looks at the entire picture, at the man or the woman who is the centre of the proceeding. It is evident, in our view, that the bare charges would certainly sustain the recommended sentence, and that is of course the understanding that both the Defence and we entered into it. It was at all times made clear that evidence of mitigation would be the centrepiece of this particular hearing and of all evidence to go before the Chamber, as well as the balance that must be struck so that this type of conduct does not happen again and that there is a deterrent value to whatever sentence the Chamber sees fit to pronounce. We recognise that it is a matter which is soundly within the discretion of the Trial Chamber. It is clear from much of what was heard today that the incidents themselves have and continue to circulate in the Admiral's consciousness and it is likely that they will stay with him until his days are over. It is equally clear that the victims and their families, and particular through families of the decedents, will have to live with the same consequences with different explanations circulating in their beings. The purpose, again - and this Chamber is well familiar with the jurisprudence of sentencing - would suggest that taking the gravity of the offence, which indeed is present, particularly where he who lets go of a weapon and allows a projectile to fire without knowing exactly who will be hit bears perhaps sometimes a heavier responsibility than a one-to-one face-to-face crime. It's the distance, the sanitisation, that perhaps adds a dimension of horror to the crime. Having said that, we have heard that at the time the Admiral recognised that it had been done wrongly. Did that make it any better or easier for those persons whose children were killed? No. Does it -- did it help at the time Dubrovnik? No. Did it contribute to anything at the time? No. Except -- it kept the dialogue going because of the responsibility which the Admiral demonstrated for the acts of his subordinates. It is noteworthy that the Croatian counterparts recognised that and deemed his resumption of negotiations as sincere. A very difficult position for both parties, the distress level being at perhaps its apex. Having said all of this, it is clear that this is perhaps a case of first impression in the Tribunal, as stated earlier, the Admiral is the first and the highest-ranking JNA officer to have entered into a negotiation without really trying to seek any type of "yes, but, yes, but"; he has simply indicated, "Yes. It happened and this is way it happened and I take responsibility for it." The guidance that our jurisprudence offers will rest with this Honourable Panel. We have hoped that bringing in some of the witnesses - and I am not at liberty, of course, to discuss in public session some of the issues that were discussed - but that this bringing in of witnesses has provided a beneficial background and understanding of some of the points that I'm sure were lingering in the minds of all of the Judges. We are hopeful that this may be the first of a number of, shall we say, initiations of recognition of the need to be responsible, and perhaps not so much that the work of the Tribunal will be rendered easier but, rather, that the work of reconciliation, which is the ultimate goal of the Tribunal, will be furthered. There is little, I think, to comment on that has not been raised. The level of cooperation of the Defence, I would like to bring to the Chamber's attention, it has been, indeed, a difficult time for both sides, and there has been absolute cooperation, in terms of working together to make this particular proceeding run seamlessly. There has been no, we use the term, "stone-walling" by attempts to side-step anything that should have been brought to the Chamber's attention. This is a full, transparent body of what we know about the events and the role of the Admiral in the events. And it has been a long way in coming out. The comment that Mr. Stefanovic made I found very telling. Whether or not the Admiral had retired or whether he was still at the end of his service, association with parties which stand for principles which at the time were not necessarily in the -- the forefront or high on the list of popularity with governments going through wars I think is significant. The comments by the Prosecution's witnesses I think will also indicate that the type of factors, the thinking outside the box, as one would say, was also evident in the course of discussions with the Admiral. Again, no one can undo the horrific damage done; no one can change the lives of those affected. No one can necessarily make Dubrovnik, the old town, what it was prior to December 6th, and nor can anyone try one try to justify anything that happened. It has been a very complex process to get an open picture of what happened, and I hope we are well on the way to presenting it, as clearly the case is not over in other parts of the Tribunal. But it is very important that those persons from the Croatian side and those persons from the former JNA side make a concerted effort to establish or help us establish the true record, and it can only serve to further the goal of the reconciliation which was so much an issue, particularly in the areas effected and in this indictment. I thank the cooperation of the Chamber's staff. It has been -- the process of the plea agreement generally is not an easy one, and we have -- I'm sure I speak for the Defence -- found a very welcoming assist from staff members, and we appreciate it. And we hope that in the future, should we have further types of negotiations along this vein, we're confident that the fairness of the Chamber and the assistance will continue. I thank you very much. I'm hopeful that the presentation on behalf of those who lost has been conveyed adequately so that, albeit you didn't have a full trial to look at, that was not the purpose of the exercise; it was so that you could understand the parameters and the depth of what happened. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber has had the opportunity to read the written submissions filed by the parties on the 14th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you for one thing. If there would be at any moment any need to go into private session because you'd like to discuss parts of the evidence presented in closed session this morning, please indicate so and we'll decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I will advise you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And today witnesses for the Prosecution and the Defence have appeared before you. We have just heard from the Prosecution and prior to my friend's eloquent speech, Admiral Jokic addressed you. At the conclusion of this hearing, a person of good will can only be struck by the senseless, unjustified, and illegal tragedy which occurred in the old town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December, 1991, claiming two lives, injuring three others, and causing damage and destruction to the most vulnerable part of the city, known as the "Pearl of the Adriatic." Your Honour, a person of goodwill seeks the truth and honesty. He attempts to demonstrate integrity, respect for authority, and honour in his dealings with others; he treats others fairly and respectfully. He is prepared to recognise his faults and failings; and in the face of adversity, he will accept the consequences of his actions in a courageous, forthright, and dignified manner. A person of goodwill will ultimately judge others and ask to be judged based on individual conduct and the content of his character. Admiral Jokic is a man of goodwill and a proud career naval officer whose admission of guilt for the events of the 6th of December, 1991, must be measured against what you have heard about his life, his character, his values, and his personality. The Chamber now knows much more about the man who pleaded guilty before you in August. Through the testimony of retired Rear Admiral Pogacnik, you know that Admiral Jokic was a respected naval officer. Both men have known each other professionally and personally for over 20 years. Mr. Pogacnik was the deputy commander to Admiral Jokic in the 9th Naval Sector in the 1980s. Their zone of responsibility in the Adriatic included the Municipality of Dubrovnik. He described Admiral Jokic as a capable and fair commander who was respected and respectful to both superiors and subordinates. Admiral Jokic was considered a successful career naval officer who through hard work earned the respect of his men and who attempted to solve problems as they arose through dialogue. On a more personal level, Mr. Pogacnik knew Admiral Jokic to be a dedicated family man. He never knew Admiral Jokic to be a nationalist, and quite to the contrary, as an officer of JNA Admiral Jokic described himself as a "Yugoslav," not in terms of ethnic or religious identity. The two men sat together at the fateful 14th Congress of the League of Communists - the final congress of the League of Communists - which marked the beginning of the end of Communism, the SFRY, and the JNA. Admiral Jokic favoured a peaceful solution to the political crisis facing his country, and indeed Mr. Pogacnik and Admiral Jokic were the only members of the JNA delegation to vote in favour of the continued confederal order within the SFRY and a peaceful solution to the looming crisis. The Trial Chamber now knows the circumstances surrounding the assignment of Admiral Jokic to Dubrovnik on the 8th of October, 1991, for on the 5th of October that year, Krsto Djurovic, the commander of the 9th Naval Sector, was killed when his helicopter went down. Admiral Jokic was ordered to replace Djurovic. He never sought the appointment and never asked to return as commander of the 9th Naval Sector. But after the death of Djurovic, Admiral Jokic was the obvious choice, since he had been the chief of staff of the 9th Naval Sector between 1977 and 1980 and the commander of the 9th Naval Sector between 1983 and 1989. Your Honour, on those fateful days in Dubrovnik in December 1991, Admiral Jokic worked closely with Mr. Davorin Rudolph, the Croatian Minister for Maritime Affairs and Minister Of Foreign affairs, who was in Dubrovnik to work on the withdrawal of JNA from Croatian territory. When the delegations headed by Mr. Rudolph and Admiral Jokic met in Cavtat near Dubrovnik on December 5th, they agreed on an immediate cease-fire and on a mechanism to improve the lives of the citizens of Dubrovnik. On the 6th of December at approximately 1400 hours, Mr. Rudolph received the radiogram from Admiral Jokic which contained an apology from Admiral Jokic for the shelling of the old town of Dubrovnik which was taking place on that day. Mr. Rudolph read out the first text of the apology on the radio to the citizens of Dubrovnik. The following day, December 7th, Mr. Rudolph and his delegation again met in Cavtat, near Dubrovnik, with Admiral Jokic, during which a final agreement and cease-fire was concluded. We say it was no small matter and a reflection of the man's character that Admiral Jokic secured the anchoring rope on Mr. Rudolph's vessel when he arrived in Cavtat. During this meeting with Mr. Rudolph, Admiral Jokic stood and in a visibly sincere manner apologised for the events of the 6th of December. Mr. Rudolph considered Admiral Jokic a willing, sincere, and genuine negotiator. He believed that Admiral Jokic negotiated in good faith and that his apology, his conduct in both face-to-face talks and his gestures during negotiations accurately reflect Admiral Jokic's character and demeanour. As the Prosecution acknowledges, the radiogram sent by Admiral Jokic to Mr. Rudolph on the 6th of December demonstrates his sincere remorse. In addition, we submit that the conduct of Admiral Jokic between the 5th and the 7th of December, in relation to Mr. Rudolph, should be considered benevolent acts, which were Admiral Jokic's attempt to change and improve the course of events. Admiral Jokic's good faith negotiations with Mr. Rudolph, which resulted in the final agreement and cease-fire, saved lives, misery, and the destruction of property. Since that time, Admiral Jokic has participated in other endeavours and activities which demonstrate his constructive social and political outlook. Mr. Stefanovic, the founding member of New Democracy, testified to these activities. As you heard Mr. Stefanovic say, New Democracy was a European-looking political party, based on liberal democratic platforms of free trade, political institutions, and respect for human rights. And Admiral Jokic was the president of the Board for Defence and Security, a consultant on military issues. He contributed significantly to the initiative for having FRY join Partnership for Peace and worked on proposals for the reform of the military and of the police. And you also heard that, in particular, Admiral Jokic was a public spokesman, an advocate in public forums organised by New Democracy concerning these initiatives. Although in a private capacity, we say that the participation of Admiral Jokic in street demonstrations in Belgrade in 1996 is significant. Here was the presence of a former senior JNA officer in the streets demonstrating against the regime. The Trial Chamber is quite familiar with Admiral Jokic's attitude towards this institution. As you know, he has voluntarily surrendered to this Court on the 12th of November, 2001. He was the first officer of the former JNA from Serbia to do so - and this, as you have heard, without the framework of the law on cooperation between the FRY and the ICTY. We say that the surrender of Admiral Jokic reflects his character and personal integrity as a man and as a soldier and his respect for authority and orders of this Tribunal. And through acts of voluntary surrender, Admiral Jokic gained the support and respect of others in government. Your Honours know that while on provisional release, Admiral Jokic's conduct has been exemplary. The commander of the UNDU reports that Admiral Jokic always conducted himself appropriately in full respect for staff and regulations. When Admiral Jokic was granted provisional release to Serbia in February 2002, he remained there, in full conformity of the guidelines imposed by the Trial Chamber. And when Admiral Jokic was allowed to travel to Montenegro to a medical institute for rehabilitation, again he remained in full compliance where the terms and conditions. And most recently, as you know, Admiral Jokic has continued to be in full compliance with his provision release conditions which you granted following his guilty plea in August. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal recognises that a plea of guilt by an accused has value and merit for the process of international criminal justice. Admiral Jokic's guilty plea and admission of guilt demonstrates his honesty. We say that his acknowledgment of the crimes and personal accountability will continue to rendering justice to victims, deter others, provide a basis for a reconciliation, and it will preclude revisionism. Entering a plea of guilty prior to the commencement of the trial makes a considerable contribution to the public advantage and work of this Tribunal. The Trial Chamber in the Plavsic case accepted that acknowledgments and full disclosure of crimes are very important when establishing the truth in relation to such crimes and that, together with acceptance of responsibility for these wrongs, it will promote reconciliation among the people in the former Yugoslavia. In particular, the plea of guilt and acknowledgment of responsibility of Admiral Jokic as a high-ranking officer in the former JNA extends to the core mission of this Tribunal, to restore peace and security to the region through accountability and reconciliation. The sincerity of his conduct and remorse cannot be in doubt. He first expressed it in the radiogram sent to the Croatian minister on the 6th of December, 1991. Admiral Jokic repeated his apology face to face with the minister the following day. And again today, in this courtroom, Admiral Jokic has expressed his regret for the tragic events of the 6th of December, in his hope for a better future. Mr. President, at this time I would like to go into private session for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. O'Sullivan, before doing so, I'm looking at the clock. We might run out of the tape in the next five to ten minutes. I deprived you already from a break between the argument of the Prosecution, because a break was planned in between, but since we are certainly not behind schedule, if you would prefer to have a break at this moment, fine. If you'd say I'd rather finish now, then I don't know how much time is left, Madam Registrar. Thirty minutes there? So we could finish. I see that the tapes have become longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We'll finish very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again, as far as I can see on my screen. Please proceed, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me conclude by saying that in addition to reviewing the sentencing briefs filed by the parties, the Chamber has now had the benefit of hearing the evidence presented by the parties at this sentencing hearing. Admiral Jokic pleaded guilty and acknowledged his responsibility for his actions as commander of the JNA 9th Naval Sector for the events that occurred in the old town of Dubrovnik on December 6th, 1991, the unlawful shelling of the old town. At the conclusion of this hearing, you know about the situation in which Admiral Jokic found himself some 12 years ago in Dubrovnik. You know what he did. You know what he failed to do, and that he did not do enough. And against the acknowledgment of responsibility, there exists substantial mitigation in the case of Admiral Jokic: His admission of guilt; his substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor; his expression of remorse; his voluntary surrender; his conduct while in detention and on provisional release; his advanced age; his conduct at the time of the crimes and after the crimes; his personal and family circumstances; his good character; his acknowledgment of the facts and the consequences of his admission of guilt, which support the Tribunal in achieving its fundamental goals: Establishing the truth, rendering justice to victims, deterring further crimes, restoring peace and security to the region through accountability and reconciliation. The significance and symbolism of any sentence imposed on Admiral Jokic must be placed in the light of his conduct, positive and negative. It must be seen in regards to its potential impact on the decisions of other accused and unknown perpetrators to come forth and face justice. In the end, Your Honour, we say that any sentence imposed on Admiral Jokic should be less than two years of imprisonment. Those are my closing remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Jokic, much has been said today. You addressed the Chamber. Is there any other issue you would like to raise at this very moment which will be the last moment to address the Chamber before we'll deliberate?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to briefly address the parties. A sentencing hearing serves to assist the Chamber when the Chamber has to determine sentence. The Chamber feels that the parties have avoided to present stereotypes or stereotypical positions which are not always of great assistance for a Chamber when a Chamber has to determine sentence, but have impressed the Chamber in what seems to be a true effort to give the assistance the Chamber needs. Before closing this hearing, I would like to go into private session for a very short moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that there's nothing any more that the parties would like to raise at this very moment. I don't see any reaction, so I take it that's true. The Chamber will deliberate. The Chamber will deliver a sentencing judgement in due course, presumably not before the recess, the December recess. We stay adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.45 p.m.
